141.title: Rows and spaces
141.hook: shoulder to shoulder in rows; men's and women's spaces are arranged differently in different communities
141.howItsDone: In congregational prayer Muslims stand in straight rows, shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, filling the front rows first; women's spaces are arranged differently in different mosques, from rows behind the men to balconies or separate rooms.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mihrab, the niche that shows which way to face, and the minbar beside it. Your line was everyone faces the same way.

On a crowded bus or train, how much space do you leave between you and a stranger? Most people leave a gap. A bag on the seat. An elbow tucked in. A careful few inches that say: not together. Then the call to stand is given in the mosque, and something happens that surprises first-time visitors. People move toward each other. Strangers close the space, until shoulders touch and the sides of their feet meet. A businessman next to a taxi driver next to a student. Today: saff.
screen: `THE CAREFUL FEW INCHES.` → `STRANGERS MOVE TOWARD EACH OTHER.` → `SHOULDERS TOUCH.`

segments.voice: Before the prayer begins, the imam often turns and says: straighten your rows, and close the gaps. It comes straight from the hadith. Bukhari and Muslim report the Prophet ﷺ saying that straightening the rows is part of completing the prayer. The companion Anas described what it looked like: each of them would put his shoulder against his companion's shoulder and his foot against his foot. A report in Abu Dawud tells them not to leave gaps for Shaytan to slip into. Another, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, warns that crooked rows lead to divided hearts. The line on the floor is also a line between people. And there are no reserved seats. Whoever comes first stands at the front; if the powerful arrive late, they stand at the back. Then the other half of the picture: where do women pray? In the Prophet's own mosque, women came to the prayers, including the dawn prayer in the dark, and prayed in rows behind the men, in the same room. Bukhari and Muslim report him saying: do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah. Today the arrangement varies a great deal. Some mosques have women's rows at the back of the same hall; some have a balcony, a side room, or a screen or curtain. Around the Ka'ba itself, men and women pray in the same open space. Muslims discuss, and sometimes argue about, which arrangement serves people best, and different communities answer differently. What doesn't change is the row itself: shoulder to shoulder, no gaps, everyone in it equal.
screen: `STRAIGHTEN YOUR ROWS.` · `SHOULDER TO SHOULDER, FOOT TO FOOT.` · `NO RESERVED SEATS.` · `WOMEN'S SPACES VARY BY COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `CLOSE THE GAP.`

segments.voice: If someone is with you, stand beside them, shoulders just touching, facing the same way; if you're alone, stand near a wall and let your shoulder rest against it. Notice the urge to pull in, to make yourself smaller, to leave a safe inch. Let your shoulders settle at their natural width instead, and take up exactly the room you take up, no more, no less.
Saff, the prayer row: shoulder to shoulder with no gaps, and the women's and men's spaces arranged in different ways by different communities.
Your line: close the gap. No reserved seats in the row, and no safe inch. Until tomorrow.

142.title: Greeting the mosque
142.hook: two short units on arriving, a greeting for the house (Bukhari)
142.howItsDone: On entering a mosque, Muslims are taught to pray two short rak'ahs before sitting, called tahiyyat al-masjid; if the congregational prayer is starting, they join it instead, and schools differ on praying it during the Friday sermon.

segments.voice: Yesterday: saff, shoulder to shoulder with no reserved seats. Your line was close the gap.

This week you've walked all the way into a mosque. Shoes off, right foot in, asking for the doors of mercy. Washed at the low taps. Found the niche that shows the way, and the steps for the sermon. Stood in a row with no gaps. Now you're inside, there's a carpet, and you'd like to sit down. Plenty of places have a small hello before you settle in: a bow at the edge of a judo mat, a nod to the room before a meeting starts. A mosque has its own. Today: greeting the mosque.
screen: `A WEEK OF WALKING IN.` → `YOU'D LIKE TO SIT DOWN.` → `FIRST, SAY HELLO.`

segments.voice: It's called tahiyyat al-masjid, the greeting of the mosque. Tahiyyah means a greeting, the same word used for the greetings in the sitting of the prayer. Bukhari and Muslim report, from the companion Abu Qatadah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: when one of you enters the mosque, let him pray two rak'ahs before he sits down. Two short units of prayer: standing, bowing, prostrating, twice, then the peace to both sides. A minute or two, then you sit. A story in Sahih Muslim shows how seriously he meant it. One Friday, while the Prophet was giving the sermon, a man named Sulayk came in and sat straight down. The Prophet stopped and asked him: did you pray two rak'ahs? He said no. The Prophet told him: stand, and pray two, and keep them short. In the middle of the sermon. Scholars have worked out the details, and they don't all agree. They generally hold that if the congregational prayer is already starting, joining it is enough. The Hanafi and Maliki schools say not to pray it once the Friday sermon has begun, reading the Sulayk story as a special case; the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools say to pray it, briefly. They also differ about the times of day when voluntary prayer is usually avoided. Why greet a building? Not because the walls are holy, but because of who the house is for. Some scholars explain it as greeting the Lord of the house before you greet anyone in it. You come in from traffic and email, and your first act inside isn't to check your phone. It's to bow.
screen: `TAHIYYAH — A GREETING.` · `TWO RAK'AHS BEFORE YOU SIT.` · `SULAYK, IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SERMON.` · `THE SCHOOLS DIFFER ON THE DETAILS.` · then, large: `YOUR FIRST ACT INSIDE IS A BOW.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you can stand now and pray two short rak'ahs, as a greeting for wherever you are. If you don't, plan a visit instead: which mosque, which day; some mosques hold open days, and it's fine to call ahead. Either way, finish by sitting still and picturing the walk in: shoes off, right foot first, water, the niche, the rows, and your first act inside a greeting.
Tahiyyat al-masjid. The greeting of the mosque: two short units of prayer on arriving, before you sit down. Today's word.
Your line: greet the house. Not the walls, but the one the house is for. Day one hundred forty-two, done.

143.title: Halal and haram
143.hook: permitted and forbidden, with most of life in the wide permitted middle
143.howItsDone: Muslims sort actions into required, recommended, permitted, disliked and forbidden, treating most everyday things as permitted unless a clear text forbids them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tahiyyat al-masjid, two short units before you sit. Your line was greet the house.

You've seen the word on a butcher's window, a food truck, a candy wrapper. Halal. If you only know it from signs, you might picture Islam as one long list of don'ts. No pork. No alcohol. No this, no that. People new to the faith sometimes feel it too: a nervous sense that every choice is a test and every snack a trap. This week looks at halal plainly, and the first thing to know is where the weight actually sits.
screen: `THE WORD ON THE BUTCHER'S WINDOW.` → `ONE LONG LIST OF DON'TS?` → `WHERE DOES THE WEIGHT SIT?`

segments.voice: Arabic dictionaries, like Lane's, tie halal to a root meaning to untie, to release. What's halal has been let loose, made free for you. Haram comes from a root meaning set apart, protected, the same root as al-Haram, the sanctuary in Mecca. Something haram is fenced off. Between the two lies nearly everything. Islamic law sorts actions into five grades: required, recommended, simply permitted, disliked, and forbidden. The simply permitted, mubah, is enormous: walking, laughing, most food, most work, a nap, a joke. And the law books state a principle for everyday things: the starting point is permission. You don't need a verse to allow a mango. You'd need one to forbid it. Surah al-Baqarah says: He it is Who created for you all that is in the earth. For you. And a report in Tirmidhi says that what Allah is silent about, He has pardoned. Sahih al-Bukhari tells of people who went the other way. Three men asked about the Prophet's worship and decided they had to outdo it. One would pray all night, every night. One would fast every day. One would never marry. When the Prophet ﷺ heard, he said: I fast, and I eat. I pray, and I sleep. I marry. And whoever turns away from my way is not of me. The forbidden list is real, but it's short. The fence is around a small field. The rest of the land is open.
screen: `HALAL — UNTIED, LET LOOSE.` · `HARAM — SET APART, FENCED.` · `FIVE GRADES, A HUGE MIDDLE.` · `I FAST, AND I EAT.` · then, large: `A SMALL FENCE, AN OPEN LAND.`

segments.voice: Name, slowly, five good things in your life that no one anywhere would call forbidden: a hot shower, your kid's laugh, the first sip of coffee, a walk, a friend's voice. Count them on your fingers, and let each one land for a breath. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah after each; if not, just notice how wide that open land is, and how much of your day it already covers.
Halal. Permitted, released, let loose: the wide open middle of life, with the forbidden fenced off at the edges. Today's word.
Your line: most things are allowed. A small choice doesn't have to be a trap. See you tomorrow.

144.title: Is it haram to date?
144.hook: the most-asked question: what's agreed, what's discussed, and why a feeling isn't a sin
144.howItsDone: Many Muslim families and communities encourage getting to know a possible spouse with marriage in mind, through introductions, family involvement, public meetings or marriage-focused apps, and keep physical closeness for marriage; where the lines fall varies by family and teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday: halal, from a root of untying. Your line was most things are allowed.

It's the question a lot of young Muslims ask a search bar before they'd ever ask a parent: is it haram to date? Sometimes it comes with a name attached. Someone from chemistry class. Someone from the group chat. Sometimes it isn't really about rules at all, but about a feeling, and whether having it makes you a bad person. The answers online tend to shout. Here's the calmer version: what's agreed, what's discussed, and what isn't a sin at all.
screen: `IS IT HARAM TO DATE?` → `SOMETIMES, A NAME ATTACHED.` → `AGREED, DISCUSSED, AND NOT A SIN.`

segments.voice: Start with what nearly every Muslim scholar agrees on. Sex belongs inside marriage, nikah. The Qur'an puts it as a fence, not just a rule: “And come not near unto adultery. Lo! it is an abomination and an evil way.” Come not near. That's why many teachers also advise against being secluded alone together; a hadith in Tirmidhi says that when a man and a woman are alone, the third with them is Shaytan. Now what's discussed. Dating, the way movies use the word, usually means a private relationship, with no plan, and physical closeness. Most scholars say that's outside the lines. But getting to know someone for marriage is different, and the hadith encourage it. A companion told the Prophet ﷺ he'd proposed to a woman. Have you seen her? the Prophet asked. No. Go and look at her, he said, for that is more likely to make things last between you. That's in Tirmidhi. So how do people meet and talk? Here, communities draw the line in different places. Some families arrange introductions. Some allow conversations with a parent or chaperone nearby, or in public places. Some people use apps built for marriage. Many call it getting to know someone with intention. Your own family and teachers will have a view, and they won't all match. And the part people most need to hear: a feeling isn't a sin. Camp two met the hadith that Allah forgives what the soul whispers, as long as it isn't acted on. Liking someone is human. And Ibn Majah reports the Prophet saying: nothing has been seen like marriage, for two people who love each other.
screen: `AGREED: CLOSENESS BELONGS IN NIKAH.` · `GO AND LOOK AT HER: ENCOURAGED.` · `HOW TO MEET: FAMILIES DIFFER.` · `A FEELING ISN'T A SIN.`

segments.voice: Think of a strong pull you're carrying: a crush, a craving, the urge to send a message at midnight. Don't push it away, and don't follow it; let it sit beside you, the way you'd sit beside a friend who's upset. On each breath out, feel the space between the feeling and the act, and notice you're still the one choosing.
Nikah. Marriage, the contract that makes a home of two people; the place the tradition gives to closeness, and the reason for getting to know someone.
Your line: a feeling isn't a sin. What you do with it is the choice. That's day one hundred forty-four.

145.title: The name on the meat
145.hook: the animal is killed swiftly, with Allah's name, a sharp blade, and mercy
145.howItsDone: Halal meat comes from an animal slaughtered with Allah's name spoken, one swift cut with a sharp blade, the blood drained, and care to spare it suffering; Muslims also say bismillah before eating.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nikah, and the question of dating: what's agreed, and what's discussed. Your line was a feeling isn't a sin.

Supermarket meat arrives on a foam tray under plastic, and the moment the animal died is somebody else's business. Islam doesn't let that moment disappear. Halal meat isn't just about which animals. It's about how. There's a name that has to be said, and a blade that has to be sharp. And a hadith puts one word over the whole thing, a word you wouldn't expect at a slaughterhouse.
screen: `A FOAM TRAY UNDER PLASTIC.` → `NOT JUST WHICH ANIMAL, BUT HOW.` → `A WORD YOU WOULDN'T EXPECT.`

segments.voice: The word is dhabihah, an animal slaughtered in the prescribed way. The core is simple. The one slaughtering says the name of Allah, usually bismillah, Allahu akbar. Then one swift cut across the throat with a very sharp blade, so it's over quickly and the blood drains out, since the Qur'an forbids eating blood. The name comes from the Qur'an: in Surah al-An'am, believers are told to eat of what Allah's name has been said over, and not of what it hasn't. Some teachers explain the name as a reminder that the life being taken was never ours: it's taken with permission, not by right. Then the word. Sahih Muslim reports, from Shaddad ibn Aws, that the Prophet ﷺ said: Allah has written ihsan on everything. Ihsan means excellence, beauty, doing a thing as well as it can be done. So when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade, and spare the animal suffering. Other reports go further: don't sharpen the knife where the animal can see, and don't slaughter one animal in front of another. The same collections tell of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and a woman punished for starving a cat. Mercy even here, at the hardest moment. Muslims differ on some modern questions: scholars disagree about stunning before slaughter, and about whether ordinary meat from Jews and Christians, whose food the Qur'an calls lawful, still counts today. Under the debates sit the plain basics: say the name, keep the blade sharp, and be kind.
screen: `DHABIHAH — THE NAME AND THE CUT.` · `EAT WHAT HIS NAME WAS SAID OVER.` · `IHSAN IS WRITTEN ON EVERYTHING.` · `SCHOLARS DIFFER ON MODERN QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `MERCY EVEN HERE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari reports that the Prophet told a young boy at his table: say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you. So picture your next meal, and pause before the first bite. If you pray, you can say bismillah, in the name of Allah; if not, remember that something, a plant or an animal, went into this plate, and someone grew it, caught it or cooked it, and give one breath of thanks.
Dhabihah. Meat slaughtered in the prescribed way: Allah's name, a swift cut with a sharp blade, and mercy. Today's word.
Your line: mercy even here. Ihsan is written on everything, even this. Day one hundred forty-five, done.

146.title: Intoxicants set aside
146.hook: wine and intoxicants are set aside because their harm outweighs their benefit (2:219; 5:90)
146.howItsDone: Muslims abstain from alcohol and other intoxicants, following 5:90 and the hadith that every intoxicant is khamr; most scholars extend this to drugs that cloud the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhabihah, the name, the sharp blade and the mercy. Your line was mercy even here.

Picture a town where almost everyone drinks. Wine at dinner, wine at weddings, poems written in its praise, merchants who make their living from it. Now picture that town giving it up. Not over a generation, with campaigns and fines. In an afternoon. A report in Bukhari says that when the final word came, the companion Anas was pouring drinks at a gathering. Someone called out the news, and they poured the jars out, until wine ran in the streets of Medina. How does a whole town get there? Slowly, and then all at once.
screen: `A TOWN WHERE EVERYONE DRINKS.` → `GIVEN UP IN AN AFTERNOON.` → `WINE IN THE STREETS OF MEDINA.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is khamr, usually translated wine or strong drink. Its root means to cover, the same root as khimar, a woman's head covering. The companion Umar explained it in Bukhari: khamr is whatever covers the mind. The Qur'an didn't forbid it all at once. First, in Surah al-Baqarah, people ask about strong drink and gambling, and the answer weighs them: there's some benefit in them for people, but, in Pickthall's words, the sin of them is greater than their usefulness. An honest scale, not a slammed door. Later, Surah an-Nisa tells believers not to come to prayer while intoxicated. Finally, Surah al-Ma'idah, verse ninety, calls strong drink, gambling and idols a work of Shaytan, and says: Leave it aside in order that ye may succeed. That's when the jars were poured out. Aisha, in Bukhari, reflected on the order. If the first verses to come down had said, don't drink wine, people would have said, we will never give it up. Hearts were prepared first. Rules came later. Muslims take the prohibition as settled. Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ saying every intoxicant is khamr, so most scholars apply it to anything that clouds the mind the same way, including drugs, and discuss medical exceptions carefully. And it's a rule Muslims keep for themselves, not a reason to look down on anyone else at the table. Underneath is the point Umar named. The mind is what you pray with, choose with, and love with.
screen: `KHAMR — WHATEVER COVERS THE MIND.` · `FIRST, AN HONEST SCALE.` · `THEN: NOT TO PRAYER INTOXICATED.` · `LEAVE IT ASIDE.` · then, large: `HEARTS FIRST, RULES LATER.`

segments.voice: Ask honestly: what covers my mind most days? It may not be a drink at all: the phone at midnight, anger that's been simmering, too little sleep, a feed that leaves you foggy. Name one without fixing it, and notice how the room feels with a clear head right now; if you pray, you can ask for help with it.
Khamr. Wine and anything that covers the mind, set aside in the Qur'an because its harm outweighs its benefit. Today's word.
Your line: keep the mind clear. It took a whole town one afternoon, after years of preparing hearts. Until tomorrow.

147.title: The gray area
147.hook: between the clear halal and clear haram are doubtful things, and whoever avoids them protects himself (Nawawi 6)
147.tomorrow: Music, tattoos, and scholars who differ
147.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to avoid matters they are unsure about, following the hadith of the doubtful things (Nawawi 6) and 'leave what makes you doubt', while scholars also warn against excessive scrupulosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khamr, whatever covers the mind. Your line was keep the mind clear.

Some choices are easy. Some are obviously wrong. And then there's the middle drawer. The email you're not sure you should forward. The deal that's legal but feels a little slippery. The ingredient on the label you can't pronounce. The joke that might be fine. There's a small itch in the chest, and no sure answer. Islam has a name for what's in that drawer, and a well-known hadith about it.
screen: `EASY, WRONG, AND THE MIDDLE DRAWER.` → `A SMALL ITCH IN YOUR CHEST.` → `ISLAM HAS A NAME FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Bukhari and Muslim report it from the companion al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, and Imam al-Nawawi placed it sixth in his collection known as the Forty. The Prophet ﷺ said: the halal is clear, and the haram is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that many people don't know. Whoever guards against the doubtful things has kept his religion and his honor safe. Then comes a picture from herding life: a shepherd grazing his flock right around the edge of a private pasture, a fenced reserve. Sooner or later the sheep wander in. Every king has his reserve, the Prophet said, and Allah's reserve is what He has forbidden. And the hadith ends somewhere unexpected: in the body there is a piece of flesh. If it's sound, the whole body is sound. If it's corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. It is the heart. The gray area is judged from the inside. There's a shorter version too. Tirmidhi reports the Prophet's grandson al-Hasan remembering these words: leave what makes you doubt for what doesn't make you doubt. And a separate report in Muslim says: sin is what wavers in your chest, and you'd hate for people to see. Two warnings keep this in balance. Remember day one hundred forty-three: most things are allowed. The gray area is a drawer, not the whole house. And scholars warn against the opposite illness, too: turning every choice into an anxious test. The point isn't fear. The hadith points to that itch in the chest.
screen: `CLEAR, CLEAR, AND DOUBTFUL BETWEEN.` · `THE SHEPHERD AT THE EDGE.` · `IT IS THE HEART.` · `A DRAWER, NOT THE WHOLE HOUSE.` · then, large: `LEAVE WHAT MAKES YOU DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Put a hand on your chest if you like, and scan the day ahead for one thing in the middle drawer: a purchase, a message, a shortcut, a conversation you're not sure about. Let the itch come, even before you can name it. Then decide, gently, to leave that one for the thing that doesn't make you doubt: no drama, no guilt, just a small step back from the edge of the pasture.
Mushtabihat, the doubtful matters between the clear halal and the clear haram, where the heart is the guide.
Your line: leave what makes you doubt. The gray area is a drawer, not the whole house. That's day one hundred forty-seven.
